title: Compound Interest
subtitle: Quantitative Aptitude – Placement Preparation
description: Learn compound interest, amount, annual and half-yearly compounding, changing interest rates, growth and depreciation, comparison with simple interest and placement-test shortcuts.
learningObjectives: Understand the meaning of compound interest.
Distinguish between simple interest and compound interest.
Calculate the compound amount and compound interest.
Find principal, rate and time in compound-interest problems.
Calculate compound interest for two and three years.
Solve half-yearly and quarterly compounding questions.
Solve questions involving different rates in different years.
Find the difference between simple interest and compound interest.
Use placement-test shortcuts for compound-interest questions.

sections.heading: 1. Basic Concept of Compound Interest
content: Compound Interest is calculated on the original principal and also on the interest accumulated during earlier periods.
At the end of every compounding period, the interest is added to the principal.
The new amount becomes the principal for the next compounding period.
Compound interest therefore produces interest on interest.

examples.question: A principal of $5,000 grows to $6,050 after a certain period. Find the compound interest.
The compound interest on a sum is $1,440 and the principal is $8,000. Find the final amount.

sections.heading: 2. Compound Amount Formula
content: The compound amount is calculated by multiplying the principal by the growth factor for every compounding period.
For annual compounding, the growth factor is 1 plus the annual rate expressed as a decimal.
After calculating the amount, subtract the principal to obtain compound interest.

examples.question: Find the amount on $5,000 at 10% per annum compounded annually for 2 years.
Find the compound interest on $8,000 at 5% per annum for 2 years.

sections.heading: 3. Year-by-Year Method
content: Compound interest can also be calculated by finding the interest separately for each year.
After every year, add the interest to the existing amount.
The resulting amount becomes the principal for the following year.
This method is useful when the rates change from year to year.

examples.question: Find the compound interest on $10,000 at 10% per annum for 2 years using the year-by-year method.
examples.solution: First-year interest = $1,000, so the amount becomes $11,000. Second-year interest = 10% of $11,000 = $1,100. Total CI = $1,000 + $1,100 = $2,100.

examples.question: Find the amount on $4,000 at 5% per annum for 3 years.
examples.solution: After year 1: $4,200. After year 2: $4,410. After year 3: $4,630.50. Therefore, the amount is $4,630.50.

sections.heading: 4. Compound Interest for Two Years
content: For two years, compound interest can be calculated using the standard amount formula.
A direct expansion formula is also useful in placement questions.
The additional term in compound interest represents interest earned on the first year's interest.
formulas: Difference between CI and SI for 2 years = PR^2/10000

examples.question: Find the compound interest on $10,000 at 10% per annum for 2 years.
Find the difference between compound interest and simple interest on $20,000 at 5% for 2 years.

sections.heading: 5. Compound Interest for Three Years
content: For three years, the amount is obtained by applying the growth factor three times.
The difference between compound interest and simple interest becomes larger as the duration increases.
The direct formula can be used when the rate remains constant.

examples.question: Find the amount on $8,000 at 10% per annum for 3 years.
Find the compound interest on $5,000 at 20% per annum for 3 years.

sections.heading: 6. Finding the Principal
content: When the final amount, rate and time are given, rearrange the compound amount formula.
Divide the amount by the complete growth factor to obtain the original principal.

examples.question: A sum becomes $12,100 in 2 years at 10% compound interest. Find the principal.
A sum becomes $9,261 in 3 years at 5% compounded annually. Find the principal.

sections.heading: 7. Finding the Rate of Interest
content: When principal, amount and time are known, compare the amount with the principal.
Find the growth factor and then determine the annual rate.
In placement questions, the growth factor often corresponds to a familiar square or cube.

examples.question: A sum of $10,000 becomes $12,100 in 2 years. Find the annual compound-interest rate.
A sum of $8,000 becomes $10,648 in 3 years. Find the rate.

sections.heading: 8. Finding the Time
content: When principal, amount and rate are given, compare the amount ratio with successive powers of the growth factor.
Placement questions generally use values that produce an exact number of years.

examples.question: In how many years will $5,000 become $6,655 at 10% compound interest?
In how many years will $10,000 become $14,641 at 10% compounded annually?

sections.heading: 9. Half-Yearly Compounding
content: When interest is compounded half-yearly, interest is calculated twice every year.
Divide the annual rate by 2 and multiply the number of years by 2.
Each half-year is treated as one compounding period.

examples.question: Find the amount on $10,000 at 10% per annum compounded half-yearly for 1 year.
examples.solution: Rate per half-year = 5% and periods = 2. A = 10,000(1.05)^2 = $11,025.

examples.question: Find the compound interest on $8,000 at 12% per annum compounded half-yearly for 1 year.

sections.heading: 10. Quarterly Compounding
content: When interest is compounded quarterly, interest is calculated four times every year.
Divide the annual rate by 4 and multiply the number of years by 4.
Each quarter is treated as one compounding period.

examples.question: Find the amount on $10,000 at 8% per annum compounded quarterly for 1 year.
examples.solution: Quarterly rate = 2% and periods = 4. A = 10,000(1.02)^4 = $10,824.32 approximately.

examples.question: Find the compound interest on $20,000 at 12% per annum compounded quarterly for 6 months.
examples.solution: Quarterly rate = 3% and the number of quarters is 2. A = 20,000(1.03)^2 = $21,218. CI = $1,218.

sections.heading: 11. Different Rates for Different Years
content: If the rate changes from one year to another, use a separate growth factor for each year.
Multiply all yearly growth factors with the original principal.
Do not use the average rate unless the question explicitly permits it.

examples.question: Find the amount on $10,000 for 2 years if the rates are 10% in the first year and 20% in the second year.
A sum of $8,000 is invested for 3 years at rates of 5%, 10% and 20% respectively. Find the amount.

sections.heading: 12. Difference Between Simple Interest and Compound Interest
content: Simple interest is calculated only on the original principal.
Compound interest includes interest on previously earned interest.
For one year, simple interest and compound interest are equal when the compounding is annual.
For more than one year, compound interest is normally greater than simple interest.

examples.question: Find the difference between CI and SI on $10,000 at 10% per annum for 2 years.
The difference between CI and SI for 2 years at 5% is $50. Find the principal.

sections.heading: 13. Finding the Rate from the Difference Between CI and SI
content: For two years, the difference between compound interest and simple interest is the interest earned on the first year's interest.
The direct difference formula can be rearranged to find the rate.

examples.question: The difference between CI and SI on $10,000 for 2 years is $144. Find the annual rate.
The difference between CI and SI on $25,000 for 2 years is $100. Find the rate.

sections.heading: 14. Successive Percentage Increase
content: Compound growth is equivalent to applying successive percentage increases.
The second increase is calculated on the increased value, not on the original value.
Two successive increases cannot normally be added directly.
formulas: Net increase for a% and b% = a + b + ab/100
Final value = Original value × (1 + a/100)(1 + b/100)

examples.question: A value increases by 10% in the first year and 20% in the second year. Find the total percentage increase.
A salary of $40,000 increases by 5% in each of two successive years. Find the salary after two years.

sections.heading: 15. Population Growth
content: Population growth follows the compound-interest model when the population increases by a fixed percentage each year.
The current population acts as the principal.
The future population is found using the compound amount formula.

examples.question: A town has a population of 50,000. It increases by 10% annually. Find the population after 2 years.
The population of a city after 2 years is 72,600. If it grows at 10% annually, find its present population.

sections.heading: 16. Depreciation
content: Depreciation represents a repeated percentage reduction in the value of an asset.
The reduced value after one year becomes the base value for the next year.
Use a reduction factor instead of a growth factor.
formulas: Depreciation amount = Original value − Final value

examples.question: A machine worth $50,000 depreciates by 10% annually. Find its value after 2 years.
A vehicle worth $80,000 depreciates by 20% per year. Find the total depreciation after 2 years.

sections.heading: 17. Growth Followed by Reduction
content: An increase followed by an equal percentage decrease does not restore the original value.
The decrease is calculated on the increased value.
The overall result is always a loss when the increase and decrease percentages are equal and non-zero.
formulas: Net change for x% increase followed by x% decrease = −x²/100%
Final value = Original value × (1 + x/100)(1 − x/100)

examples.question: A value increases by 20% and then decreases by 20%. Find the net percentage change.
examples.solution: Net change = −20²/100 = −4%. Therefore, there is a 4% decrease.

examples.question: A machine valued at $25,000 appreciates by 10% and then depreciates by 10%. Find its final value.

sections.heading: 18. Money Becoming Double or Multiple Times
content: Under compound interest, the amount grows by repeated multiplication.
To find when a sum becomes double or triple, compare the required amount ratio with powers of the growth factor.
Unlike simple interest, the time required is not found using RT = 100.

examples.question: A sum becomes double in 5 years under compound interest. In how many years will it become four times at the same rate?
examples.solution: Four times means double twice. Therefore, the required time is 5 + 5 = 10 years.

examples.question: A sum becomes three times in 8 years. In how many years will it become nine times?
examples.solution: Nine times equals 3 × 3. Therefore, the required time is 8 + 8 = 16 years.

sections.heading: 19. Ratio-Based Compound-Interest Problems
content: Compound amount ratios can often be solved without calculating the actual amounts.
When the rates and times are the same, the final amounts remain in the same ratio as the principals.
When the principals are the same, compare the growth factors.
formulas: For equal rates and times, A1 : A2 = P1 : P2

examples.question: Two principals are in the ratio 3:5 and are invested at the same compound-interest rate for the same time. Find the ratio of their amounts.
examples.solution: Since both have the same growth factor, the amount ratio remains 3:5.

examples.question: Equal sums are invested for 2 years at 10% and 20% compound interest. Find the ratio of their amounts.

sections.heading: 20. Placement-Test Strategy
content: Identify whether the question asks for principal, amount, rate, time or compound interest.
Check whether compounding is annual, half-yearly or quarterly.
Modify both the rate and number of periods when the compounding frequency changes.
Use the year-by-year method when different rates apply in different years.
Use the direct CI and SI difference formula for two-year questions.
Treat population growth as compound increase and depreciation as compound decrease.
For successive changes, multiply the factors instead of simply adding the percentages.
Estimate the answer before choosing an option.

examples.question: Find the amount on $20,000 at 10% compounded annually for 2 years.
A machine worth $60,000 depreciates by 10% annually for 2 years. Find its value.

quickShortcuts.title: Basic amount formula
quickShortcuts.note: Amount = Principal × (1 + Rate/100) raised to the number of years.

quickShortcuts.title: Find compound interest
quickShortcuts.note: Subtract the principal from the compound amount.

quickShortcuts.title: Two-year difference
quickShortcuts.note: For two years, CI − SI = Principal × Rate² ÷ 10000.

quickShortcuts.title: Half-yearly compounding
quickShortcuts.note: Halve the annual rate and double the number of periods.

quickShortcuts.title: Quarterly compounding
quickShortcuts.note: Divide the annual rate by 4 and multiply the number of periods by 4.

quickShortcuts.title: Different yearly rates
quickShortcuts.note: Multiply a separate growth factor for each year.

quickShortcuts.title: Population growth
quickShortcuts.note: Use the compound amount formula with a positive growth rate.

quickShortcuts.title: Depreciation
quickShortcuts.note: Replace the growth factor with 1 minus Rate/100.

quickShortcuts.title: Successive increases
quickShortcuts.note: For increases of a% and b%, net increase = a + b + ab/100.

quickShortcuts.title: Equal increase and decrease
quickShortcuts.note: An x% increase followed by an x% decrease results in an x²/100 percent loss.

quickShortcuts.title: Same rate and time
quickShortcuts.note: Compound amounts remain in the same ratio as the original principals.

quickShortcuts.title: Amount ratio
quickShortcuts.note: Compare principal multiplied by its complete growth factor.

quickShortcuts.title: Doubling pattern
quickShortcuts.note: If money doubles in T years, it becomes four times in 2T years.

quickShortcuts.title: Tripling pattern
quickShortcuts.note: If money triples in T years, it becomes nine times in 2T years.

quickShortcuts.title: Avoid averaging rates
quickShortcuts.note: For different yearly rates, multiply the factors instead of using the arithmetic average.

commonMistakes: Using the simple-interest formula for a compound-interest question.
Forgetting to subtract the principal when only compound interest is asked.
Giving compound interest when the question asks for the total amount.
Using the original principal for every year's interest in the year-by-year method.
Adding yearly rates instead of multiplying their growth factors.
Using the annual rate directly for half-yearly compounding.
Forgetting to double the number of periods for half-yearly compounding.
Using the annual rate directly for quarterly compounding.
Forgetting to multiply the number of periods by four for quarterly compounding.
Using RT = 100 for compound-interest doubling questions.
Treating equal percentage increase and decrease as zero net change.
Using a positive growth factor for depreciation.
Applying the two-year CI and SI difference formula to three-year questions.
Using the amount instead of the principal in the difference formula.
